## 1. Executive summary

We evaluate **TimesFM-2.5** (`google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch`, $\sim$200 M
parameters) under exactly the same parsing, scoring, and chance-correction
pipeline used for the Chronos-Bolt baseline (Appendix~D of the paper). On the
**full 469-item test split** of the three forecasting templates (L1.7, L2.4,
L2.5), TimesFM-2.5 achieves chance-corrected accuracy of **56.3 %** on L1.7,
**46.9 %** on L2.4, and **50.1 %** on L2.5 — slightly above Chronos-Bolt on
L1.7 (51.5 %), tied on L2.4 (46.9 % vs 46.9 %), and tied within bootstrap CI
on L2.5 (50.1 % vs 49.7 %). Inference takes 88 s on a single A10G GPU
(vs Chronos-Bolt's 24 s), still 2–3 orders of magnitude faster than
running an LLM panel.

Two TSFMs of comparable parameter count and pretraining-budget order produce
**substantively similar numbers** on the FactoryBench forecasting slice. This
strengthens the appendix's central claim: the result is not an artefact of the
particular TSFM chosen — it is a property of pretrained forecasters as a
class. It also keeps the second-message intact: both models can address only
3 of 21 templates.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-headline
#| echo: false
def fmt(v): return f"{v:.3f}"
rows = []
for tag in ["L1.7", "L2.4", "L2.5"]:
    t = T_TIMES["templates"][tag]
    rows.append({
        "Template": tag,
        "n": t["n"],
        "Raw mean": fmt(t["raw_mean"]),
        "Raw 95% CI": f"[{t['raw_ci_lo']:.3f}, {t['raw_ci_hi']:.3f}]",
        "Chance-corrected": fmt(t["cc_mean"]),
        "CC 95% CI": f"[{t['cc_ci_lo']:.3f}, {t['cc_ci_hi']:.3f}]",
    })
em = T_TIMES["L1.7_exact_match"]
rows.append({
    "Template": "L1.7 (exact-match)",
    "n": em["n"],
    "Raw mean": fmt(em["raw_mean"]),
    "Raw 95% CI": f"[{em['raw_ci_lo']:.3f}, {em['raw_ci_hi']:.3f}]",
    "Chance-corrected": fmt(em["cc_mean"]),
    "CC 95% CI": "—",
})
pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

## 2. Background and motivation

### 2.1 The reviewer critique (recap)

The Chronos-Bolt appendix is framed around that reviewer comment:

> *"No time-series foundation models are evaluated. The paper motivates the
> benchmark partly for evaluating 'time-series models' (it is in the abstract),
> but every evaluated model is a general-purpose LLM receiving serialized
> numerical data as text. Chronos, TimesFM, Moment are the obvious baselines."*

Chronos-Bolt addresses the first half of the request. This notebook addresses
the second half. The key concern Chronos-Bolt alone leaves open is
**robustness**: any single TSFM result invites the objection that the numbers
are model-specific. A second, independently developed TSFM that produces
substantively similar numbers shifts the claim from "this particular
forecaster is competitive" to "TSFMs as a class are competitive on the
forecasting slice."

### 2.2 Why TimesFM-2.5 specifically

We chose `google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch` because:

- **Independent of Chronos.** Different lab (Google Research vs Amazon),
  different architecture family (decoder-style with separate point and
  quantile heads vs Chronos's encoder-decoder with a 9-quantile head),
  different pretraining corpus.
- **Same parameter scale.** 200 M parameters matches Chronos-Bolt-base
  exactly; size is held fixed.
- **Same zero-shot capability.** No benchmark-specific fine-tuning
  required, matching the LLM panel setting.
- **Publicly available and well-cited.** Aligns with the second TSFM
  directly named in the paper's Related Work (`\cite{das2024decoder}`).

A multivariate TSFM (Moirai-MoE) or a non-decoder family member (Moment,
Lag-Llama) would be the next natural follow-ups; we leave them as future
work and note the limitation in §6.

### 2.3 Template applicability (recap)

A pure forecaster has neither a language interface nor a notion of options,
ranking, or counterfactual conditioning. Of the 21 question templates
released in `factorynet_qa_150k`, only three reduce to a well-posed
forecasting problem: L1.7 (state, scalar forecast), L2.4 (intervention,
scalar forecast under a known anomaly), and L2.5 (intervention, 6-joint
tensor forecast). The remaining 18 require classification, ranking,
free-form text, or counterfactual conditioning. **This 3 of 21 = 14 %
template ceiling applies to TimesFM-2.5 exactly as it does to Chronos-Bolt:**
neither model has a language head.

| Template | Level | Question type | Answer | Applicable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1.1, L1.2 | State | Anomaly / fault classification | MC | ✗ |
| L1.3 | State | Severity ranking | Ranking | ✗ |
| L1.5, L1.6 | State | Root cause / KPI effect | Free-form / MC | ✗ |
| **L1.7** | **State** | **Signal at $T+n$** | **Numerical** | ✓ |
| L2.1, L2.2 | Intervention | Effect of / choice of intervention | MC | ✗ |
| L2.3 | Intervention | Intervention ranking | Ranking | ✗ |
| **L2.4** | **Interv.** | **Signal at $T+n$ (anomalous)** | **Numerical** | ✓ |
| **L2.5** | **Interv.** | **6-joint values at $T+n$** | **Tensor[6]** | ✓ |
| L2.6 | Intervention | Effect description | Free-form | ✗ |
| L3.1–L3.6 | Counterfactual | "If X had not happened…" | MC / Ranking / FF | ✗ |
| L4.1–L4.3 | Decision | Troubleshooting, optimization | Free-form | ✗ |

### 2.4 What we hold fixed

By design, only the forecasting model changes between the Chronos and TimesFM
runs:

- **Same items** — the 469 applicable Q&A pairs from the test split.
- **Same parsing** (`parse_qa.py`) — reverse-decoded numeric arrays, target
  signal and horizon picked the same way.
- **Same scorer** (`scoring.py`) — piecewise-margin, $E=1/4$ chance
  correction.
- **Same $R/12$ margin** computed at evaluation time for L1.7, alongside the
  exact-match fallback (see §4.3).
- **Same bootstrap procedure** — 1000 resamples, percentile method, fixed
  seed `12345` (`analyze.py:RNG_SEED`); CC interval endpoints are
  $\max(0,(b-1/4)/(1-1/4))$ for the corresponding raw bootstrap quantiles.

## 3. Methodology — what differs from Chronos

We refer the reader to the Chronos appendix for the data pipeline,
template-applicability table, and scoring details. The deltas for TimesFM-2.5
are:

- **Loading.** The published `timesfm` package on PyPI requires Python <3.12
  (carries `paxml`/`lingvo` as a hard dep). We install from source
  (`pip install /tmp/timesfm-src` against the upstream Git repo) which only
  requires `numpy`, `huggingface_hub`, `safetensors`, and `torch>=2.0`. We
  also bypass the `PyTorchModelHubMixin.from_pretrained` path because the
  installed `huggingface_hub` (1.13) forwards a `proxies=` kwarg into the
  model constructor, which TimesFM 2.5's wrapper does not accept; we
  manually `hf_hub_download` the safetensors and call `load_checkpoint`
  directly. The fix is encapsulated in `run_timesfm.py:TimesFM25Forecaster`.
- **Output API.** TimesFM 2.5 returns `(point_forecast, quantile_forecast)`.
  We use the **point forecast** at the last predicted step. (Chronos-Bolt
  returns 9 quantiles; we used the median.) For both, the prediction is the
  model's canonical scalar estimate at horizon $h$.
- **Compile config.** TimesFM 2.5 requires a one-time `compile()` call with
  `(max_context, max_horizon)`. We pass `(512, 64)` so the same compiled
  graph handles every item; FactoryBench contexts are $\le 77$ steps and
  horizons $\le 10$, well within these bounds.
- **Multivariate handling for L2.5.** Same as Chronos-Bolt: 6 independent
  univariate calls, one per joint. TimesFM 2.5 has no native multivariate
  mode either.

### 4.3 L1.7 margin caveat: both scoring conventions

L1.7 items in the released dataset do **not** carry a `margin` field in
`acceptance_bounds`, so the LLM scorer falls through to **exact match**
(`|pred - gt| < 1e-4`) — essentially unattainable for a real-valued
forecast. We score TimesFM-2.5 under **both** conventions: the *intended*
$R/12$ calibration (matching how the paper calibrates tensor scoring at
chance level $E=1/4$) and the strict exact-match fallback.

```{python}
#| echo: false
em = T_TIMES["L1.7_exact_match"]
t = T_TIMES["templates"]["L1.7"]
print(f"L1.7 with R/12 margin (intended; chance level E=1/4):")
print(f"  raw {t['raw_mean']:.3f} [{t['raw_ci_lo']:.3f}, {t['raw_ci_hi']:.3f}]"
      f"  → chance-corrected {t['cc_mean']:.3f}")
print(f"L1.7 with exact-match fallback (LLM scorer's behaviour):")
print(f"  raw {em['raw_mean']:.3f} [{em['raw_ci_lo']:.3f}, {em['raw_ci_hi']:.3f}]"
      f"  → chance-corrected {max(0, (em['raw_mean']-0.25)/0.75):.3f}")
if T_CHRON is not None:
    cem = T_CHRON["L1.7_exact_match"]
    ct = T_CHRON["templates"]["L1.7"]
    print(f"\nFor comparison, Chronos-Bolt under the same two conventions:")
    print(f"  R/12:        raw {ct['raw_mean']:.3f} → cc {ct['cc_mean']:.3f}")
    print(f"  exact-match: raw {cem['raw_mean']:.3f} → cc 0.000")
```

The exact-match number ($\le 4\,\%$) is what a strict head-to-head with the
LLM pipeline would yield on L1.7. The $R/12$ number ($\sim 67\,\%$ raw,
$\sim 56\,\%$ chance-corrected) is what the *intended* calibration yields and
is what every other forecasting template (L2.4, L2.5) uses. We report both
so the reader can pick the comparison that suits their question. The
collapse to $\le 4\,\%$ for **both** TSFMs under exact match is itself
informative: it confirms the gap is a property of the **scorer**, not of
either model. Either re-running the LLM scorer with the $R/12$ margin or
shipping the margin in the released dataset would close it.

## 5. Fairness analysis — is this apples to apples?

This section mirrors §4 of the Chronos-Bolt notebook
(`report_full.qmd`) and addresses the same dimensions for TimesFM-2.5. The
asymmetries between either TSFM and the LLM panel are, by design, the same
because we hold parsing, scoring, and chance correction fixed across the
two TSFM runs.

### 5.1 What IS comparable (apples to apples)

- **Same Q&A items.** TimesFM-2.5 answers the exact same 469 questions
  drawn from the same test split.
- **Same scoring rule.** Identical margin-based piecewise scorer with the
  same chance correction ($E=1/4$).
- **Same zero-shot setting.** No fine-tuning for either TimesFM-2.5 or the
  LLMs.
- **Same ground truth.** The actual future signal value from each episode.
- **TimesFM-2.5 vs Chronos-Bolt is *fully* apples-to-apples.** Items,
  parsing, scorer, chance correction, bootstrap, and L1.7 margin are all
  held fixed; only the model changes.

### 5.2 What is NOT comparable to the LLM panel

The biggest asymmetry is the **input representation**:

- **LLMs** receive the time series as **text tokens**:
  `t=0.0: fbp0=1.50, fbs1=0.20, ...`. Values are rounded to **2 decimal
  places** (lossy), feature names are **acronymized**, and the full prompt
  also includes the question text, robot description, acronym mapping, and
  (for MCQ items) the option set. Token counts can run into the thousands.
  LLMs **know what is being asked** and can reason linguistically about
  it, including using the anomaly description on L2.4/L2.5 as a
  conditioning variable.
- **TimesFM-2.5** receives **raw float32 arrays per channel** at full
  precision, with no acronym decoding, no question text, no robot
  context, and no anomaly description. It runs **independently per
  channel** (univariate). Cross-channel reasoning is not available.

This cuts both ways:

| Dimension | Advantage |
|---|---|
| Numeric precision (raw float vs 2dp text) | **TimesFM-2.5** |
| Question awareness (knows what is asked) | **LLMs** |
| Anomaly context (L2.4/L2.5: knows what fault is present) | **LLMs** |
| Cross-channel reasoning (multivariate) | **LLMs** |
| Pretraining on real time-series data | **TimesFM-2.5** |

### 5.3 Template coverage asymmetry

TimesFM-2.5 answers **3 of 21** templates. LLM scores in the paper are
aggregated across **all** templates per level. The LLM L1 score
(e.g.\ Claude at 46.8 %) includes L1.1, L1.2, L1.3, L1.5, L1.6, *and*
L1.7 — not just L1.7. TimesFM-2.5's L1 number is **L1.7 only**. These are
not directly comparable as "L1 scores." We always label TimesFM-2.5
results as template-specific (L1.7, L2.4, L2.5), never as level-wide.

### 5.4 The L1.7 margin caveat

Detailed in §4.3. In short: L1.7 items in the released dataset don't carry
a stored margin, so the LLM scorer falls through to exact match. The TSFM
appendix evaluates both conventions and reports both numbers. Until either
the dataset stores the $R/12$ margin or the LLM scorer is re-run with it,
the L1.7 head-to-head between TSFMs and LLMs is not strictly apples-to-apples
under the strict scoring; the *internal* TSFM head-to-head between
Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM-2.5 is fully apples-to-apples regardless of
which convention is chosen, because both TSFMs are scored under the same
convention.

### 5.5 Verdict

This is a **controlled comparison on a shared subset of templates with
identical scoring**, not a head-to-head on the full benchmark. The
comparison is informative precisely because it now triangulates between
two pretrained forecasters: the TimesFM-2.5 numbers tell us that the
Chronos-Bolt result is not a single-model artefact, while the TSFM-vs-LLM
comparison still sits behind the input-representation and template-coverage
caveats. Both pieces of evidence are needed.

## 6. Interpretation

### 6.1 What the results mean for the paper

The TimesFM-2.5 numbers reinforce the three messages from the Chronos
appendix and add one new one.

1. **Reinforced.** A 200 M-parameter pretrained forecaster, evaluated zero-shot
   on the FactoryBench forecasting templates, is competitive with the best LLM
   panel level-aggregate scores: TimesFM-2.5 chance-corrected scores of
   0.56 / 0.47 / 0.50 sit at or above the Claude Sonnet 4.6 L1/L2 aggregates
   (0.47 / 0.47).
2. **Reinforced.** A pure forecaster covers only 3 of 21 templates regardless of
   which TSFM we pick — the structural limitation is not an artefact of
   Chronos-Bolt's specific architecture or training data.
3. **Reinforced.** L1.7 under the strict exact-match LLM-fallback scorer
   produces $\le 4\,\%$ raw accuracy for both Chronos and TimesFM, confirming
   that the missing L1.7 margin is a scoring-pipeline issue rather than a
   model-capability issue.
4. **New.** The agreement between the two TSFMs on the per-signal and
   per-horizon breakdowns (very similar shapes, modest TimesFM lead at short
   horizons) suggests the FactoryBench forecasting items have a model-class
   intrinsic difficulty that is not strongly modulated by which TSFM we pick.
   This is a small additional piece of evidence that the benchmark is
   measuring a stable property of the items rather than a quirk of one model.

### 6.2 Why this strengthens the paper

The TimesFM-2.5 baseline is the second piece of the response to that
reviewer's TSFM critique. Together with the Chronos-Bolt baseline it lets
the paper make three quantitative claims it could not previously support
with numbers:

- **Some pretrained forecaster is competitive with frontier LLMs on the
  forecasting slice of FactoryBench.** The Chronos-Bolt result alone made
  this claim defensible; TimesFM-2.5 alone would also have made it
  defensible. Having both makes it robust to the choice of TSFM.
- **The result is not a property of one model.** Two independently
  developed, architecturally distinct, separately pretrained TSFMs of the
  same parameter scale converge to within bootstrap CI overlap on every
  template, with the same shape of per-signal and per-horizon profile.
  This is the kind of cross-model consistency check that hardens an
  otherwise circumstantial claim.
- **The 14 % template ceiling is structural, not architectural.** Both
  TSFMs can only address 3 of 21 templates, because that is the
  forecasting subset of FactoryBench. The benchmark's value is precisely
  that it spans capabilities beyond forecasting; the rest of the templates
  measure something deeper than next-step prediction. Adding a third or
  fourth TSFM does not change this.

### 6.3 Limitations of this baseline

- Two TSFMs is more than one but still a small sample of the design space.
  Moment, Lag-Llama, and Moirai (in particular Moirai-MoE, which is
  multivariate) are obvious follow-ups using the same parsing and scoring
  pipeline.
- Univariate forecasting per channel: TimesFM-2.5 has no native multivariate
  mode, so for L2.5 we run six independent per-joint forecasts, exactly as
  in Chronos-Bolt. A multivariate TSFM might exploit cross-joint
  correlations that we explicitly disable.
- Short context: FactoryBench items are 32–77 timesteps; both TSFMs were
  trained on contexts up to 512, so this baseline likely under-uses each
  model's effective receptive field.
- L1.7 margin discrepancy from §4.3 / §5.4: until either the dataset stores
  the $R/12$ margin or the LLM scorer is re-run with it, the L1.7 row
  should be read in pairs (one row per scoring convention).
- TimesFM-specific deployment friction: the upstream PyPI package is
  pinned to Python $<$ 3.12 by `paxml`/`lingvo`. We install from source.
  If the official wheel catches up, the runner can be simplified.
- We use TimesFM-2.5's **point forecast** as the prediction (vs Chronos's
  median quantile). For Chronos-Bolt the point forecast and the median
  quantile are the same series; for TimesFM the point forecast is what
  the model emits as its canonical scalar prediction, while the quantile
  head carries 10 separate predictions. We keep the point forecast for
  consistency with the published TimesFM API; reading the median quantile
  (`out[1][:,:,5]`) produces numerically very similar results in spot
  checks but we have not characterised the difference at the population
  level.

## 7. Reproducibility

```bash
# Same data files as the Chronos run.
cd experiments/v1
python download_data.py
python run_timesfm.py \
    --input data/level_1_test.jsonl data/level_2_test.jsonl \
    --max-per-template 999999 \
    --output results_timesfm.json \
    --device cuda
python analyze.py --results results_timesfm.json --prefix timesfm_
quarto render report_timesfm.qmd
```

End-to-end on a single A10G: under two minutes including model load.

Artifacts:

- `results_timesfm.json` — per-item predictions + scores (469 items)
- `timesfm_analysis_summary.json` — aggregates, CIs, breakdowns
- `report_timesfm.html` — this notebook rendered
- `timesfm_fig_*.png` — plots embedded above
